title: Has anyone gone from AI character art to a 2D run cycle you actually used in a game?
author: yaxir
selftext:
I’m making a 2D game on my own and learning animation as I go. I tried an AI video tool and liked how much weight and bounce it gave this run. The hands and clothing change shape during the clip, though, so I’m trying to get that movement with artwork I can reuse on a rig.

[https://imgur.com/a/coBmymC](https://imgur.com/a/coBmymC)

I’ve tried cutting the artwork into layers and using motion data in Unity. I can get it moving, but I’m still figuring out how much that saves if I have to fix the poses and timing afterward.

If you’ve got a character moving in an actual playable build, what did you end up doing by hand? Did starting from motion data help, or was it quicker to make a few poses yourself? A rough before-and-after would help me understand what’s realistic for one person.

comments.author: StoneCypher
comments.body: i've been having ai make custom skins for standard meshes and then animating them using mecanim and screenshotting that

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body: Thanks! Do you have a short clip or sprite sheet from one you’ve made? I’m trying to picture how much of the drawn look survives when you put it on a standard 3D model. Did the reused run animation work pretty much as-is, or did you still have to spend time getting the feet and clothes to move right?

comments.author: Dakroh_88
comments.body: I’ve kind of build a tool for this, www.keyframe.it.com 2d image to 3d then rig and animate with blender/cowork then just render out each frame from every angle. Built it as an experiment for fun but made it public, no sign up or download all in the browser

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Hey, thanks! I saw Keyframe has an MCP connector. I’m making this on my own and I don’t know how to rig or animate by hand, so I’m curious how far you’ve actually got with an agent driving it.

If I give Claude Code or Codex a layered 2D character and a reference run, can it set up the rig, make the loop, then look at the result and fix things like sliding feet or a gap opening at the elbow? Which steps did you still have to do yourself?

If you have a short demo of that workflow, I’d love to see it.

replies.author: Dakroh_88
replies.body: Yeah so agents can fully use it, I have noticed Claude cowork is better result wise than ChatGPT. Honestly if you connect imagegen (gpt cli) to your Claude then it can make its own images it works pretty well. I don’t do any of it my self, I just tell the agent the issue or show it screen shots of the issue and it’ll resolve them

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
That’s exactly what I’m hoping to do. I’m happy to point out what looks wrong. It’s the actual rigging and fixing I don’t know how to do.

When you do this in Cowork, is it using Keyframe’s MCP or driving the browser directly? And do you have a quick before-and-after of something you pointed out in a screenshot and the agent fixed? Even one elbow gap or sliding foot would be perfect.

replies.author: Dakroh_88
replies.body: Depends on what im working on, if its something small itll just connect and do it and return it back to me if im doing something like a character with a bunch of animations i useually have it just do it in its local browser so i can play it and pause it to make taking screen shots easier. But its literally just like talking to an animator, just belike fix the feet sliding, and it does. hah

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Haha, that’s exactly how I’d like to work. I can usually spot when a foot is sliding. I just don’t know what to move to fix it.

I’ll try it on one run loop. When you flag foot sliding, do you usually give the agent a short clip, or is a screenshot and “this foot should stay planted here” enough?

replies.author: Dakroh_88
replies.body: Just tell it that you don’t want the feet sliding it can usually figure it out

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body: Got it, thanks! I’ll try that on one run loop and ask it to show me the same foot plant before and after. That should make it easier for me to see what it actually fixed.

replies.author: Dakroh_88
replies.body: It’ll usually check them frame by frame

comments.author: PacificIsMyHome
comments.body: I have been using a Diablo 2 style pipeline. It's a paper doll system with layers for clothes armor weapons ECT, but done in 3d in blender for the bases and animations then baked into sprite sheets. Everything is tinted by GODOT so skintone, clothing color weapon and armor color are all swappable on the fly.  Claud MCP to GODOT and runs blender headless with a plugin.  I am able to get the variety I want and use available 3d animations with some tweaking.

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body: That sounds really useful for getting variety out of one rig. Do you have a short clip of a finished character running, ideally with two outfits on the same animation? I’d love to see how the layers hold together in motion. What took the most manual work on the first character, and how much of that could you reuse on the next one?

replies.author: PacificIsMyHome
replies.body:
I don't have anything recorded right now, but I can grab something if you are interested.  
My goal is to have 3 bases Male, Female, and a gender agnostic "beast person" with packages for heads hands and feet and skin texture for lizard folk, were wolves etc.
Each base will have all the animations.  The base becomes all characters.  Swappable faces (including ears) and scaling make all the variety-- this is where I am right now.  Can I make a dwarf by displaying my base at full width and ~55% height? Can I make an elf with a face package that has the ears and is ~10% skinnier and slightly taller and still get clean looking characters?  So far the answer is maybe.

The manual work is tweaking and customizeing animations for the right feel.  Once they are good everything else is layers and display tricks (hopefully)

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body:
Yeah, I’d love to see it! A rough screen recording is plenty. If you already have two outfits or body shapes working, seeing the same run on both would be really helpful. One is fine too.

I’m still learning animation, so if there’s one thing you changed in the original run that made it feel better, I’d love to know what it was. I can usually tell when a run looks stiff, but I don’t yet know what to change to fix it. Thanks for offering to record it!!

replies.author: PacificIsMyHome
replies.body: There were some weird things like shoulders being too far back.  I am have walking cleaned up a little, I don't think I have even touched run yet, so as far as running goes it's still rough and doesn't look great. (I know this is what you were asking for). I will see if I can get .gif(s) to spit out or something to show you.  This is all very much a work in progress, but I have test layers to show off for outfits (not game finished quality, but proof of concept stuff) I have a walk in a circle and swap layers test scene I can tweak to spit out a .gif (I think).  Animations still need tweaking, but if I only have to animate 3 bases that is a hell of a lot easier than doing a bunch of them.

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body: Yeah, the walk-and-outfit-swap test would be great! I’d love to see what happens when the outfit changes mid-step. A rough GIF of what you already have is plenty. No need to clean up the run for me. thx for offering to grab it!

replies.author: PacificIsMyHome
replies.body:
So this is what I have still tweaking things, and obviously none of this is game ready yet, but it's moving in that dirrection with a few more tweaks.

replies.author: PacificIsMyHome
replies.body: I am working on an Isometric, and it looks like you are on a side scroller, but I think the pipe line would work the same

comments.author: MakingSoulStudio
comments.body: Hit the same wall making a character swing their arm in Godot. 3D didn't fit my art style, Codex wasn't good at 2D rigging, and sprites always had that choppy look. Didn't solve it either, so I'm following this one.

replies.author: yaxir
replies.body: Yeah, that’s exactly the wall I’m hitting too. Getting the arm to move is one thing. Getting it to feel like it belongs to a person is another. I’ll share what works if I get a good result.

comments.author: Sea-Routine6045
comments.body: The solution is making 3D models. Rigging, Animating and then RENDERING them as 2D sprites with custom shaders to make it look like whatever art style you are looking for.
